text: John Timothy Griffin, born August 21, 1968, is an American lawyer and politician serving as the 57th attorney general of Arkansas. He previously served as the 20th lieutenant governor of Arkansas from 2015 to 2023. A member of the Republican Party, Griffin was the United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Arkansas from 2006 to 2007 and represented Arkansas's 2nd congressional district from 2011 to 2015. He defeated Democrat John Burkhalter for lieutenant governor in 2014 and served under Governor Asa Hutchinson. In summer 2020, Griffin announced his candidacy for the 2022 Arkansas gubernatorial election but withdrew in February 2021, subsequently launching a successful campaign for Arkansas Attorney General. Born in Charlotte, North Carolina, and raised in Magnolia, Columbia County, southern Arkansas, Griffin graduated from Hendrix College, attended Pembroke College, Oxford, and earned his Juris Doctor from Tulane Law School. From September 1995 to January 1997, he worked with Special Prosecutor David Barrett in the investigation of former HUD Secretary Henry Cisneros. He then served as Senior Investigative Counsel for the House Committee on Government Reform for two years. In September 1999, he became Deputy Research Director for the Republican National Committee (for George W. Bush's election campaign) and served as a legal advisor for the "Bush-Cheney 2000 Florida Recount Team" (Bush v. Gore). From March 2001 to June 2002, he was a special assistant to Assistant Attorney General Michael Chertoff. From June 2002 to December 2004, he was Research Director and Deputy Communications Director for Bush's 2004 reelection campaign. In June 2007, Senators Edward Kennedy and Sheldon Whitehouse asked the U.S. Justice Department to investigate whether Griffin led an RNC effort to suppress the African-American vote in Jacksonville, Florida, through caging during the 2004 election; Griffin called the allegations "absolutely, positively false," and no wrongdoing was found. In April 2005, Griffin began working in the George W. Bush administration as Karl Rove's aide, with the title of Special Assistant to the President and Deputy Director in the Office of Political Affairs. In September 2006, after completing a one-year military assignment, he became a special assistant to U.S. Attorney Bud Cummins in the Eastern District of Arkansas. On December 15, 2006, the Justice Department announced Griffin would be appointed interim U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Arkansas, effective December 20, 2006. Before a March 2006 revision to the Patriot Act, interim U.S. Attorneys had a 120-day term limit pending Senate confirmation; after the revision, interim appointees had no term limit, effectively bypassing Senate confirmation if the President declined to nominate. Griffin was among the first group of interim attorneys appointed without a term limit by Attorney General Gonzales. Gonzales's decision particularly angered then-Democratic senators Blanche Lincoln and Mark Pryor, who stated Gonzales had promised them Griffin would go before the Senate for confirmation. On May 30, 2007, Griffin resigned effective June 1, 2007, delivering a tearful speech stating public service was "not worth it" and that he was married with a child, apologizing for putting his wife through it and expressing a desire to move on. Documents from a congressional investigation revealed that White House officials wanted a vacancy in the U.S. Attorney's office in Little Rock to appoint Griffin, who was a top Republican researcher and aide to Rove. On February 16, 2007, ten days after McNulty testified Cummins resigned under duress to create a vacancy for Griffin, Griffin announced he would not seek the presidential nomination to be U.S. Attorney in Little Rock. In September 2008, the Department of Justice's Office of Inspector General concluded Cummins had not been removed for performance reasons but to make room for Griffin. On August 11, 2009, The New York Times reported previously classified White House emails showing Karl Rove had lobbied for Griffin to succeed Cummins. On May 31, 2007, The Washington Post reported speculation that Griffin was in discussions with the then-nascent presidential campaign of Fred Thompson for a top-level post; Griffin denied any such discussions and stated he had not spoken to GOP leadership or the McCain campaign. In September 2009, Griffin announced he was running for Congress to replace Democrat Vic Snyder, who stepped down after fourteen years in Arkansas' 2nd congressional district. He defeated Democratic nominee Joyce Elliott, the outgoing Majority Leader of the Arkansas Senate, winning 58% of the vote. Griffin won re-election with 55% of the vote over former state representative Herb Rule. In 2009, Griffin signed a pledge sponsored by Americans for Prosperity promising to vote against any global warming legislation that would raise taxes. In response to the Obama Administration's decision, then House Majority Leader Eric Cantor announced Congress would need to approve any delay; Griffin argued that although he believed the administration's unilateral delay of the mandate was illegal, he still believed it was a good way to save jobs and protect workers. Griffin served on various committees and subcommittees, including the House Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security, where on January 16, 2014, he challenged statistics presented by Carolyn Colvin, the acting commissioner of the Social Security Administration, who claimed 99 percent of disability payments were correctly made without fraud. Griffin was the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor in 2014, defeating two Republican challengers, Andy Mayberry and Debra Hobbs, in the primary with 63 percent of the vote. In the general election on November 4, 2014, he defeated Democrat John Burkhalter. Griffin won re-election in the 2018 general election. He attends Immanuel Baptist Church, a Southern Baptist congregation in Little Rock.
